text: With the help of a diagram, show how the tilt of the Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun cause the seasons and the variation in the length of day and night.
modelAnswer: The Earth's axis is permanently tilted at 23.5 degrees to the perpendicular of its orbital plane, and this tilt stays fixed in direction as the Earth revolves around the Sun each year. Because of this tilt, different parts of the Earth lean towards or away from the Sun at different points in the orbit. Around 21 June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun's rays fall more vertically there, giving it summer with longer days and shorter nights, while the Southern Hemisphere, tilted away, has winter with shorter days. Around 22 December, the situation reverses: the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun and has summer, while the Northern Hemisphere has winter. At the equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September), neither hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the circle of illumination passes through both poles, and every place on Earth has equal (12 hours) day and night. A simple diagram would show the Earth at four positions around its orbit, with the axis tilted at a constant 23.5 degrees and the circle of illumination cutting across differently at each position.
keyPoints: Axis is permanently tilted at 23.5 degrees and keeps the same direction throughout the year
Around 21 June: Northern Hemisphere tilts towards Sun -> summer, long days; Southern Hemisphere -> winter, short days
Around 22 December: reverse situation -> Southern Hemisphere summer, Northern Hemisphere winter
At equinoxes, no hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so day and night are equal (12 hours) everywhere

text: Draw a neat and labelled diagram of the Heat Zones of the world, and briefly describe each zone.
modelAnswer: The Earth's surface is divided into three main heat zones based on latitude and the angle of the Sun's rays: (1) The Torrid (Tropical) Zone lies between the Tropic of Cancer (23.5 degrees N) and the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5 degrees S); it receives the most direct, nearly vertical rays of the Sun throughout the year and so is the hottest zone. (2) The Temperate Zones lie between the Tropics and the Arctic/Antarctic Circles (66.5 degrees N and S); they receive the Sun's rays at a more slanting angle and experience four distinct seasons with moderate temperatures. (3) The Frigid (Polar) Zones lie beyond the Arctic and Antarctic Circles towards the poles; they receive highly oblique sunlight (and experience long periods of continuous daylight or darkness), making them the coldest zones. A diagram would show the globe with the Equator at the centre, the Tropic lines on either side marking the Torrid Zone, the Arctic/Antarctic Circle lines marking the edges of the Temperate Zones, and the polar caps labelled as the Frigid Zones.
keyPoints: Torrid Zone: between the Tropics, hottest, nearly vertical sun rays all year
North/South Temperate Zones: between Tropics and Arctic/Antarctic Circles, moderate, four seasons
North/South Frigid Zones: beyond the Arctic/Antarctic Circles, coldest, oblique sunlight and long polar day/night

text: Write three points of difference between the Summer Solstice and the Winter Solstice.
modelAnswer: The Summer Solstice (around 21 June) occurs when the Sun's vertical rays fall on the Tropic of Cancer, whereas the Winter Solstice (around 22 December) occurs when the vertical rays fall on the Tropic of Capricorn. During the Summer Solstice, the Northern Hemisphere experiences its longest day and shortest night of the year, while during the Winter Solstice it experiences its shortest day and longest night. Correspondingly, during the Summer Solstice the Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day, while during the Winter Solstice the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day — the two hemispheres always experience opposite seasons at the solstices.
keyPoints: Summer Solstice (21 June): vertical rays over Tropic of Cancer; Winter Solstice (22 Dec): vertical rays over Tropic of Capricorn
Summer Solstice gives Northern Hemisphere its longest day/shortest night; Winter Solstice gives it the shortest day/longest night
The two hemispheres always have opposite day-length conditions at the two solstices

text: Why does the International Date Line (IDL) exist, and what happens to the date of a traveller who crosses it from west to east, compared to one who crosses it from east to west?
modelAnswer: The IDL exists because, as a traveller moves eastward around the Earth crossing time zones, they keep advancing their clocks and would eventually gain a full day compared to someone who stayed in one place; similarly, travelling westward they would keep losing time and fall a day behind. The IDL (roughly along 180 degrees longitude) is the fixed line at which this accumulated difference is corrected. A traveller crossing the IDL from west to east (for example, from Asia towards America) must subtract one day from the calendar date, while a traveller crossing it from east to west must add one day, so that the entire world stays consistent in its reckoning of dates.
keyPoints: IDL corrects the day gained/lost from continuously changing time zones while travelling around the world
Crossing west to east: subtract one calendar day
Crossing east to west: add one calendar day
Keeps the whole world's calendar date consistent

text: With the help of a diagram, describe the structure of the Earth's interior, naming its main layers and their key characteristics.
modelAnswer: The Earth's interior is made up of three main concentric layers. The Crust is the thin, solid outermost layer, varying from about 5-10 km thick under the oceans to 30-40 km under the continents; it is composed of a lighter upper SIAL layer (silica and aluminium rich, e.g. granite) and a denser lower SIMA layer (silica and magnesium rich, e.g. basalt). Below the crust lies the Mantle, separated from it by the Moho discontinuity; it is about 2,900 km thick, made of dense silicate rock, and includes the partly molten asthenosphere in its upper part. At the centre lies the Core, separated from the mantle by the Gutenberg discontinuity; it is composed mainly of iron and nickel (the NIFE layer) and consists of a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, the latter solid despite extreme temperature because of immense pressure. A labelled diagram would show these layers as concentric circles/shells, from the thin crust on the outside to the solid inner core at the very centre, with the Moho and Gutenberg discontinuities marked at the appropriate boundaries.
keyPoints: Crust: thin, solid, outermost; SIAL (upper) and SIMA (lower) sub-layers
Mantle: thick (~2900 km), dense silicate rock, includes the asthenosphere; separated from crust by Moho discontinuity
Core: innermost, iron-nickel (NIFE); liquid outer core, solid inner core; separated from mantle by Gutenberg discontinuity

text: Differentiate between the crust's SIAL and SIMA layers (give three points).
modelAnswer: SIAL is the upper layer of the Earth's crust, composed mainly of silica and aluminium-rich rocks such as granite; it forms the continental crust, is comparatively lighter in density (around 2.7 g/cm3), and is thicker under the continents. SIMA is the lower layer of the crust, composed mainly of silica and magnesium-rich rocks such as basalt; it forms the floor of the ocean basins as well as underlying the SIAL on continents, is denser (around 3.0 g/cm3) than SIAL, and is found as a continuous layer across the whole Earth, unlike SIAL which is absent under much of the ocean floor.
keyPoints: SIAL: silica-aluminium rich (granite), lighter, forms continental crust
SIMA: silica-magnesium rich (basalt), denser than SIAL, forms ocean floor and underlies SIAL
SIMA is continuous worldwide; SIAL is present mainly under continents, largely absent under oceans

text: Explain the Rock Cycle with the help of a diagram, describing how the three main types of rock are interconverted.
modelAnswer: The rock cycle describes the continuous transformation of rock from one type to another over geological time, with no fixed beginning or end. Molten magma from within the Earth cools and solidifies to form Igneous rock (e.g. granite, basalt). When exposed at the surface, igneous (as well as sedimentary and metamorphic) rocks are broken down by weathering and erosion into sediment, which is transported, deposited in layers and compacted/cemented to form Sedimentary rock (e.g. sandstone, limestone). When sedimentary (or igneous) rock is subjected to great heat and pressure deep within the Earth, often near plate boundaries, it is altered without melting into Metamorphic rock (e.g. slate, marble). If metamorphic (or any) rock is pushed deep enough to melt completely, it becomes magma again, ready to restart the cycle as a new igneous rock. A diagram would show magma at the centre with arrows looping out to igneous rock, then to sediment/sedimentary rock through weathering and deposition, then to metamorphic rock through heat and pressure, and back to magma through melting, forming a continuous circular cycle.
keyPoints: Magma cools and solidifies -> Igneous rock
Weathering, erosion, deposition and compaction of any rock -> Sedimentary rock
Heat and pressure acting on any rock (without melting) -> Metamorphic rock
Complete melting of any rock -> magma again, restarting the cycle (no beginning or end)

text: What is Metamorphism? State its main causes and name two types of metamorphism.
modelAnswer: Metamorphism is the process by which an existing rock (igneous, sedimentary, or even another metamorphic rock) is altered in its mineral composition, texture or structure, without completely melting, usually deep within the Earth's crust. It is mainly caused by intense heat (from nearby magma or the Earth's internal temperature), great pressure (from overlying rock layers or tectonic movement), and sometimes chemically active fluids. Two common types of metamorphism are Thermal (contact) metamorphism, caused mainly by heat from nearby magma intrusions, and Dynamic metamorphism, caused mainly by intense pressure from tectonic plate movement, such as during mountain building.
keyPoints: Metamorphism: alteration of existing rock by heat/pressure, without melting
Causes: heat, pressure, and chemically active fluids
Thermal (contact) metamorphism: caused mainly by heat from nearby magma
Dynamic metamorphism: caused mainly by pressure from tectonic movement

text: With reference to Igneous rocks, classify them on the basis of (a) place/depth of solidification and (b) silica content, giving one example in each category.
modelAnswer: On the basis of where they solidify, igneous rocks are of three types: Plutonic rocks (e.g. granite), which solidify very slowly deep within the Earth and have large crystals; Hypabyssal rocks (e.g. dolerite), which solidify at intermediate depths, cooling faster and forming medium-sized crystals; and Volcanic (extrusive) rocks (e.g. basalt), which solidify rapidly at or near the surface, forming fine-grained or glassy rock. On the basis of silica content, igneous rocks are classified as Acidic rocks (e.g. granite), which contain more than 65% silica, are lighter in colour, and are less dense; and Basic rocks (e.g. basalt, gabbro), which contain less silica (around 45-55%), are darker in colour, and are denser.
keyPoints: Plutonic (e.g. granite): solidify deep, very slowly, large crystals
Hypabyssal (e.g. dolerite): solidify at intermediate depth, medium crystals
Volcanic/extrusive (e.g. basalt): solidify at/near surface, fine-grained
Acidic rocks (e.g. granite, high silica, light) vs Basic rocks (e.g. basalt, low silica, dark, dense)

text: Give two points of difference between Block mountains and Fold mountains.
modelAnswer: Block mountains are formed by faulting, where the land on either side of a fault subsides or a block of land is uplifted along fault lines, leaving the block standing as a mountain with steep, straight sides (e.g. the Vosges mountains in Europe). Fold mountains, on the other hand, are formed by the folding of rock layers under intense compressional force when two tectonic plates collide, producing long, curving mountain ranges with alternating upfolds (anticlines) and downfolds (synclines), and are generally much higher and more extensive (e.g. the Himalayas, the Alps).
keyPoints: Block mountains: formed by faulting, steep straight sides, e.g. Vosges
Fold mountains: formed by compressional folding of rock layers, curving ranges with anticlines/synclines, e.g. Himalayas
Fold mountains are generally higher and more extensive than block mountains

text: How does the movement of tectonic plates on the Earth's surface lead to the formation of mountains?
modelAnswer: The Earth's crust is broken into several large tectonic plates that float on the partly molten asthenosphere and move very slowly due to convection currents in the mantle. When two plates move towards each other and collide, the immense compressional force at the boundary causes the rock layers between them to buckle and fold upward, forming fold mountains (e.g. the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates formed the Himalayas). Where plates move apart or slide past one another, the resulting tension can cause faulting, which, together with the uplift or subsidence of blocks of land, forms block mountains. In both cases, it is the slow but continuous movement of these rigid plates against or away from each other that provides the compressional or tensional forces responsible for mountain building.
keyPoints: Earth's crust is divided into plates that move slowly due to mantle convection
Colliding plates compress and fold rock layers upward -> fold mountains (e.g. Himalayas from India-Eurasia collision)
Plates moving apart/sliding past each other cause faulting and block uplift -> block mountains

text: Differentiate between Mechanical weathering and Chemical weathering (two points).
modelAnswer: Mechanical (physical) weathering is the breaking down of rocks into smaller pieces by physical forces such as temperature change, frost action and salt crystal growth, without any change in the chemical composition of the rock; it is most active in hot deserts and cold regions with large temperature ranges. Chemical weathering is the decomposition of rocks through chemical reactions such as oxidation, carbonation, hydration and solution, which change the mineral composition of the rock; it is most active in warm, humid regions where water and heat speed up the reactions.
keyPoints: Mechanical: physical breakdown, no change in chemical composition
Chemical: decomposition by chemical reactions, composition changes
Mechanical dominant in deserts/cold regions; chemical dominant in warm, humid regions

text: Give two differences between Oxidation and Carbonation as processes of chemical weathering.
modelAnswer: Oxidation is the reaction of oxygen (in air or dissolved in water) with minerals in a rock, especially iron-bearing minerals, forming oxides (rust); it gives rocks a reddish-brown or yellowish colour and makes them brittle. Carbonation is the reaction of carbonic acid (carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater) with rocks containing calcium carbonate, such as limestone and chalk; it dissolves the rock and is responsible for the formation of caves, stalactites and stalagmites in limestone regions.
keyPoints: Oxidation: oxygen reacts with iron minerals -> rust, reddish colour, brittle rock
Carbonation: carbonic acid reacts with calcium carbonate rocks (limestone)
Carbonation dissolves rock and forms caves, stalactites and stalagmites

text: Discuss three factors that are highly responsible for mechanical weathering.
modelAnswer: (1) Temperature change: in hot deserts, rocks expand during the hot day and contract during the cold night; repeated expansion and contraction causes exfoliation (peeling of outer layers), block disintegration or granular disintegration. (2) Frost action: in cold and temperate regions, water entering rock cracks freezes and expands by about 9%, widening the cracks; repeated freezing and thawing eventually breaks the rock apart. (3) Biological/organic action: plant roots growing into rock cracks widen them, and burrowing animals loosen rock fragments. Other contributing factors include the nature and structure of the rock (rocks with joints, vertical layers or dark minerals weather faster) and salt crystal growth in arid regions.
keyPoints: Temperature change: alternate expansion and contraction -> exfoliation, block/granular disintegration
Frost action: freezing and thawing of water in cracks widens and splits rock
Plant roots and animals widen cracks and loosen rock
Rock structure (joints, vertical layers, dark minerals) also influences rate

text: Briefly explain the meaning of (i) Granular disintegration and (ii) Block disintegration.
modelAnswer: (i) Granular disintegration occurs in coarse-grained rocks such as granite that are made of different minerals; because each mineral expands and contracts at a different rate when heated and cooled, the bonds between grains weaken and the rock crumbles into individual grains. (ii) Block disintegration occurs in rocks with many joints, especially in hot deserts; repeated expansion and contraction along the joints causes the rock to break apart into rectangular blocks.
keyPoints: Granular disintegration: different minerals expand/contract at different rates; rock crumbles into grains
Common in coarse-grained rocks like granite
Block disintegration: jointed rocks split into rectangular blocks along joints
Both caused by temperature change, mainly in hot deserts

text: Describe the three stages of a river's course and the main features formed in each stage.
modelAnswer: (1) Upper (youthful) course: the river flows swiftly down a steep slope and erodes mainly downward (vertical erosion); features include V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons, rapids and waterfalls. (2) Middle (mature) course: the slope becomes gentler, the volume of water increases and lateral (sideways) erosion dominates; the river develops meanders and ox-bow lakes and begins depositing material, forming floodplains. (3) Lower (old) course: the river flows very slowly over an almost flat plain, carrying a heavy load; deposition dominates, forming wide floodplains, levees, braided channels, and finally a delta or an estuary at its mouth.
keyPoints: Upper course: steep slope, vertical erosion; V-shaped valleys, gorges, rapids, waterfalls
Middle course: gentler slope, lateral erosion; meanders, ox-bow lakes, floodplains begin
Lower course: slow flow, deposition dominates; floodplains, levees, deltas/estuaries

text: (a) Name the crescent-shaped dunes found in the Sahara Desert. (b) How are these dunes formed? (c) Describe their structure.
modelAnswer: (a) Barkhans (Barchans). (b) They form where wind blows steadily from one direction over a flat, hard surface with a limited supply of sand; sand piles up around a small obstacle and the wind sweeps the edges forward faster than the centre, producing a crescent. (c) A barkhan has a gentle, convex windward slope facing the wind and a steep, concave leeward (slip) face; its two horns (tips) point downwind, in the direction the wind is blowing. Barkhans migrate slowly downwind as sand is blown up the windward slope and slides down the slip face.
keyPoints: Name: Barkhans/Barchans
Formed by steady one-directional wind over a flat surface with limited sand
Gentle windward slope; steep leeward slip face
Horns point downwind; dunes migrate in the wind's direction

text: Mention two differences between Seif (longitudinal) dunes and Barkhan dunes.
modelAnswer: Seif dunes are long, narrow, sharp-crested ridges of sand that lie parallel to the direction of the prevailing wind and can stretch for many kilometres; they form where winds blow from a fairly constant direction with some cross-winds. Barkhans are crescent-shaped dunes that lie transverse (at right angles) to the wind direction, with horns pointing downwind; they are usually isolated and much smaller, and form where the wind blows steadily from one direction over a flat surface with limited sand.
keyPoints: Seif: long ridges parallel to wind direction
Barkhan: crescent-shaped, transverse to wind, horns point downwind
Seifs are long and extensive; barkhans are usually smaller and isolated

text: Why are mushroom rocks commonly found in desert regions? Explain how they are formed.
modelAnswer: In deserts, strong winds carry sand grains that act as tools, sand-blasting (abrading) rock surfaces. Since the heaviest sand grains are carried close to the ground (within about 1-2 m), the lower part of an exposed rock is eroded much faster than its upper part. Over time the base is undercut while the top remains broad, giving the rock the shape of a mushroom (a pedestal rock). The lack of vegetation and dry, loose sand in deserts allows this wind abrasion to operate strongly.
keyPoints: Wind-borne sand abrades (sand-blasts) rock surfaces
Most sand is carried close to the ground, so the base is eroded faster
Undercut base and broader top produce a mushroom shape
Absence of vegetation and loose dry sand make deserts ideal

text: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the intrusive volcanic features: sill, dyke, laccolith and batholith.
modelAnswer: When magma rises but solidifies below the Earth's surface, it forms intrusive features. (1) Sill: a horizontal sheet of igneous rock formed when magma spreads out and solidifies between and parallel to existing rock layers. (2) Dyke: a vertical or steeply inclined wall-like sheet of igneous rock formed when magma solidifies in a crack cutting across rock layers. (3) Laccolith: a dome-shaped (mushroom-like) mass formed when viscous magma intrudes between rock layers and pushes the overlying strata upward into a dome, with a flat base. (4) Batholith: a huge, irregular, dome-shaped mass of igneous rock (usually granite) that solidifies deep within the crust; it often forms the core of mountain ranges and becomes exposed after the overlying rocks are eroded. A diagram would show a volcano cone with a vent connected to a deep batholith/magma chamber, a horizontal sill and a vertical dyke branching off, and a dome-shaped laccolith raising the layers above it.
keyPoints: Sill: horizontal sheet parallel to rock layers
Dyke: vertical wall-like sheet cutting across rock layers
Laccolith: dome-shaped intrusion arching overlying layers, flat base
Batholith: huge deep-seated granite mass forming the core of mountains

text: With the help of a diagram, explain the terms Focus, Epicentre and Seismic waves in relation to an earthquake.
modelAnswer: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the release of energy within the crust. The Focus (hypocentre) is the point inside the Earth where the rocks first rupture and from which the energy is released. The Epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus; it is the first place on the surface to receive the shock and usually experiences the greatest damage. Seismic waves are the waves of energy that radiate outward in all directions from the focus; they include Primary (P) waves, the fastest, which travel through solids and liquids; Secondary (S) waves, which travel only through solids; and Surface (L) waves, which travel along the surface and cause the most damage. A diagram would show the focus below the surface, the epicentre directly above it, and concentric wave fronts spreading out from the focus.
keyPoints: Focus: point inside the Earth where the earthquake originates
Epicentre: point on the surface directly above the focus; maximum damage
Seismic waves radiate outward from the focus
P waves (fastest, solids and liquids), S waves (solids only), L/surface waves (most destructive)

text: Discuss the destructive effects of earthquakes, and state one positive effect.
modelAnswer: Destructive effects: (1) collapse of buildings, bridges, dams and roads, causing great loss of life and property; (2) landslides and avalanches in hilly regions; (3) tsunamis when earthquakes occur beneath the sea, flooding coastal areas; (4) fires caused by broken gas lines and electric wires; (5) disruption of water supply, communication and transport, and changes in river courses. Positive effects: earthquakes may raise new land, create lakes or expose mineral deposits, give rise to springs, and help scientists understand the Earth's interior through the study of seismic waves.
keyPoints: Collapse of buildings and infrastructure; loss of life and property
Landslides, avalanches, fires and tsunamis
Disruption of water, transport and communication; river courses may change
Positive: new landforms/lakes, exposure of minerals, springs, knowledge of the interior

text: State two constructive effects of volcanoes.
modelAnswer: (1) Volcanic lava weathers into very fertile soil (e.g. the black soil of the Deccan Plateau), which is good for agriculture. (2) Volcanic activity creates new landforms such as islands, mountains and plateaus (e.g. the Hawaiian Islands, the Deccan Plateau). Volcanoes also bring valuable minerals to the surface, provide geothermal energy and hot springs, and attract tourists.
keyPoints: Lava weathers into fertile soil (e.g. black soil of the Deccan)
Creates new landforms: islands, volcanic mountains, plateaus
Brings minerals to the surface; geothermal energy; hot springs; tourism

text: Mention two adverse effects of a volcanic eruption.
modelAnswer: (1) Lava flows, hot ash and poisonous gases destroy settlements, crops and forests and can cause heavy loss of human and animal life (e.g. Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in 79 A.D.). (2) Ash and gases released into the atmosphere pollute the air, disrupt air transport and can lower global temperatures for a time. Eruptions may also trigger earthquakes, mudflows and tsunamis.
keyPoints: Lava, ash and poisonous gases destroy life, property, crops and forests
Ash and gases pollute the atmosphere and disrupt air travel; may cool climate
Can trigger earthquakes, mudflows and tsunamis

text: Mention one difference between explosive and quiet types of volcanic eruption, and name two products erupted by a volcano.
modelAnswer: An explosive eruption occurs when thick, viscous, silica-rich (acidic) magma traps gases, which build up pressure and are released violently, throwing out ash, rock fragments and gases, and forming steep-sided cones (e.g. Mt. Vesuvius). A quiet (fissure) eruption occurs when thin, fluid, basic lava with little trapped gas flows out gently through cracks or vents, spreading over large areas and forming lava plateaus or shield volcanoes (e.g. the Deccan Plateau, Mauna Loa). Products erupted by volcanoes include lava, volcanic ash and dust, rock fragments (pyroclasts/volcanic bombs), steam and gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide.
keyPoints: Explosive: viscous acidic magma, trapped gases, violent; steep cones
Quiet: fluid basic lava flows gently; lava plateaus/shield volcanoes
Products: lava, ash, dust, rock fragments, steam, gases (SO2, CO2)

text: How are composite cones formed?
modelAnswer: Composite cones (stratovolcanoes) are formed by a series of alternating explosive and quiet eruptions over a long time. Each explosive eruption deposits a layer of ash, cinders and rock fragments, and each quieter eruption adds a layer of lava over it. The repeated alternation builds up a tall, steep-sided, symmetrical cone made of alternate layers (strata) of lava and ash, often with small side vents (parasitic cones). Examples are Mt. Fuji (Japan) and Mt. Vesuvius (Italy).
keyPoints: Formed by repeated alternating explosive and quiet eruptions
Alternate layers (strata) of ash/cinders and lava
Tall, steep-sided, symmetrical cones; may have parasitic cones
Examples: Mt. Fuji, Mt. Vesuvius

text: Give two differences between a cinder cone and a composite cone.
modelAnswer: A cinder (ash) cone is built mainly of ash, cinders and small rock fragments thrown out by explosive eruptions; it is small, with concave, steep slopes and a large crater, and is usually formed by a single or short-lived eruption (e.g. Paricutin in Mexico). A composite cone is built of alternating layers of lava and ash from repeated eruptions; it is much larger and taller, with a symmetrical shape, and is formed over a long period (e.g. Mt. Fuji).
keyPoints: Cinder cone: ash and cinders only; composite: alternate lava and ash layers
Cinder cone: small, short-lived; composite: large, tall, built over a long period
Examples: Paricutin (cinder), Mt. Fuji (composite)

text: Why is the Circum-Pacific belt known as the 'Ring of Fire'? Why does intense earthquake activity occur along it?
modelAnswer: The Circum-Pacific belt is a horseshoe-shaped zone around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, along the coasts of the Americas, Japan, the Philippines and New Zealand. It is called the 'Ring of Fire' because it contains about two-thirds of the world's active volcanoes. Here the Pacific Plate and other oceanic plates are subducting (sinking) beneath surrounding plates; the friction and stress at these convergent boundaries cause frequent and intense earthquakes, while the melting of the subducted plate produces magma that feeds the volcanoes.
keyPoints: Zone encircling the Pacific Ocean with about two-thirds of the world's active volcanoes
Oceanic plates subduct beneath surrounding plates at convergent boundaries
Friction/stress at boundaries causes intense earthquakes; melting plates produce magma

text: Explain any two man-made causes that can lead to an earthquake.
modelAnswer: (1) Construction of large dams and reservoirs: the enormous weight of stored water and its seepage into faults increase stress on the underlying rocks, which can trigger earthquakes (reservoir-induced seismicity, e.g. Koyna, Maharashtra, 1967). (2) Underground nuclear explosions and testing release sudden shock waves that disturb the rock layers. Other causes include deep mining and quarrying, which cause the collapse of underground cavities, and extraction of oil, gas or groundwater, or injection of fluids, which alters pressure in rock layers.
keyPoints: Large dams/reservoirs: weight and seepage of water stress faults (e.g. Koyna 1967)
Underground nuclear explosions send shock waves through rocks
Deep mining, and extraction or injection of fluids, also disturb rock layers

text: Explain any three factors responsible for the formation of ocean currents.
modelAnswer: (1) Planetary winds: prevailing winds such as the Trade Winds and Westerlies drag the surface water along in their direction, producing surface currents (e.g. the North and South Equatorial Currents). (2) Differences in temperature and salinity (density): warm water at the equator is lighter and flows towards the poles on the surface, while cold, dense polar water sinks and flows towards the equator; similarly, water of high salinity is denser and moves towards areas of low salinity. (3) Rotation of the Earth (Coriolis force): deflects currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, producing circular gyres. The shape and position of coastlines and the configuration of the ocean floor also modify the direction of currents.
keyPoints: Planetary winds drag surface water (e.g. Equatorial Currents)
Temperature and salinity differences create density differences that drive water movement
Earth's rotation (Coriolis force) deflects currents right in NH, left in SH -> gyres
Shape of coastlines and ocean floor modify direction

text: With the help of diagrams, distinguish between Spring tides and Neap tides.
modelAnswer: Spring tides occur twice a month, on new moon and full moon days, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line. The gravitational pulls of the Sun and Moon act together, so the high tide is higher and the low tide lower than usual; the tidal range is maximum. Neap tides also occur twice a month, on the 7th/8th days of the first and last quarters of the Moon, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other with respect to the Earth. Their gravitational pulls work against each other, so the high tide is lower and the low tide higher than usual; the tidal range is minimum. Diagram for spring tide: Sun, Earth and Moon in one line with the water bulging along that line. Diagram for neap tide: Moon at 90 degrees to the Sun-Earth line, with the lunar bulge partly cancelled by the solar bulge.
keyPoints: Spring tide: Sun, Moon, Earth in a straight line (new/full moon)
Spring tide: pulls combine -> highest high tides, maximum tidal range
Neap tide: Sun and Moon at right angles (first/last quarter)
Neap tide: pulls partly cancel -> low high tides, minimum tidal range

text: State two effects of tides that are helpful to man.
modelAnswer: (1) High tides raise the water level in harbours and river mouths, enabling large ships to enter and leave ports (e.g. Kolkata, London); tidal currents also help clear silt from harbours and prevent ports in cold countries from freezing. (2) Tides can be used to generate tidal energy, a renewable source of electricity, in narrow bays and estuaries. Tides also help fishermen, as fish come closer to the shore at high tide, and they help carry away sewage and waste from the coast.
keyPoints: Raise water level so ships can enter ports; clear silt; keep harbours from freezing
Tidal energy can be harnessed for electricity
Help fishing and carry away coastal waste

text: (a) What is the other name of the Kuroshio Current? Is it a warm or cold current? (b) Give two impacts of the Kuroshio Current.
modelAnswer: (a) The Kuroshio Current is also called the Japan Current or the 'Black Stream' (because of its deep blue, almost black water). It is a warm current. (b) Impacts: (1) It keeps the eastern/south-eastern coast of Japan warm even in winter and keeps its ports ice-free. (2) Where it meets the cold Oyashio Current near northern Japan, the mixing of warm and cold water produces fog but also creates one of the richest fishing grounds in the world, because of abundant plankton. It also brings moisture and rainfall to the coastal areas it passes.
keyPoints: Other names: Japan Current / Black Stream; it is warm
Keeps the east coast of Japan warm in winter; ports ice-free
Meets cold Oyashio -> fog and rich fishing grounds
Brings moisture and rainfall to coastal areas

text: How is rainfall affected by the flow of ocean currents in different parts of the world?
modelAnswer: Warm ocean currents warm the air above them; this air picks up moisture and, when it blows over the land, brings rainfall to coastal areas (e.g. the warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift give rainfall to north-western Europe). Cold ocean currents cool the air above them, making it stable and dry; winds blowing over them bring little rain, so the coasts they wash are often dry. This is why many of the world's hot deserts, such as the Atacama (cold Peru/Humboldt Current), the Namib (cold Benguela Current) and the deserts of western Australia, lie on the western margins of continents washed by cold currents.
keyPoints: Warm currents warm and moisten air -> rainfall on nearby coasts (e.g. NW Europe)
Cold currents cool and stabilise air -> little or no rainfall
Hot deserts on western margins lie along cold currents (Atacama, Namib)

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the structure of the Earth's atmosphere, giving the approximate extent and one characteristic of each layer.
modelAnswer: (1) Troposphere: from the surface up to about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator (average about 13 km); it contains most of the water vapour and dust, all weather phenomena occur here, and temperature falls by about 6.5 degrees C per km (normal lapse rate); its upper boundary is the tropopause. (2) Stratosphere: from the tropopause to about 50 km; it contains the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays, so temperature rises with height; the air is calm and free from weather disturbances, making it ideal for jet aircraft. (3) Mesosphere: from about 50 to 80 km; temperature falls with height to about -90 degrees C, the coldest part of the atmosphere; meteors burn up here. (4) Thermosphere/Ionosphere: from about 80 to 400-640 km; it contains electrically charged ions that reflect radio waves back to Earth, and auroras occur here; temperature rises sharply with height. (5) Exosphere: the outermost layer beyond about 640 km, with very thin air and no definite upper limit, gradually merging with outer space. The diagram should show these layers stacked from the surface upwards with their heights.
keyPoints: Troposphere (0-13 km avg): weather, water vapour, temperature falls with height
Stratosphere (to ~50 km): ozone layer, calm, temperature rises; jet aircraft fly here
Mesosphere (50-80 km): coldest layer, meteors burn up
Thermosphere/Ionosphere (80-640 km): ions reflect radio waves, auroras
Exosphere (beyond ~640 km): very thin air, no definite upper limit

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: What is the cause of ozone layer depletion? State one impact of ozone depletion on the environment.
modelAnswer: The main cause of ozone depletion is the release of man-made chemicals, especially chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays, along with halons and nitrogen oxides from supersonic jets. In the stratosphere, these chemicals release chlorine and bromine atoms that break down ozone molecules. Natural causes include volcanic eruptions and sunspot activity. As the ozone layer thins, more harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation reaches the Earth's surface, causing skin cancer, cataracts and weakened immunity in humans, and damaging crops, plankton and other marine life.
keyPoints: Main cause: CFCs (refrigerators, ACs, aerosols), halons, nitrogen oxides
Chlorine/bromine atoms break down ozone in the stratosphere
Natural causes: volcanic eruptions, sunspots
Impact: more UV rays -> skin cancer, cataracts, damage to crops and marine life

chapter: Air (Composition and Structure of the Atmosphere)
text: What is the importance of water vapour and dust particles in the atmosphere?
modelAnswer: Water vapour absorbs part of the incoming solar radiation and much of the outgoing terrestrial radiation, helping to keep the Earth warm (acting as a blanket); it is also the source of all forms of condensation and precipitation, such as clouds, fog, dew, rain and snow. Dust particles act as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour condenses to form cloud droplets and fog; they also scatter and reflect sunlight, producing the red and orange colours seen at sunrise and sunset.
keyPoints: Water vapour absorbs heat and keeps the Earth warm
Water vapour is the source of all condensation and precipitation
Dust particles act as condensation (hygroscopic) nuclei
Dust scatters sunlight, producing colours at sunrise and sunset

text: Explain the Heat Budget of the Earth with the help of a diagram.
modelAnswer: The heat budget is the balance between the incoming solar radiation (insolation) received by the Earth and the outgoing terrestrial radiation, which keeps the Earth's average temperature constant. If incoming insolation is taken as 100 units: about 35 units are reflected back to space directly by clouds, dust and the Earth's surface (the Earth's albedo) and do not heat the Earth; about 14 units are absorbed by the atmosphere; and about 51 units reach and are absorbed by the Earth's surface. The Earth then radiates these 51 units back as long-wave terrestrial radiation: part goes directly to space and the rest is absorbed by the atmosphere, which in turn radiates it to space. In total, the Earth-atmosphere system returns 65 units to space (17 from the surface directly and 48 from the atmosphere), equal to the 65 units absorbed, so there is no net gain or loss of heat. A diagram would show arrows for incoming insolation, reflected portion, absorbed portions, and outgoing terrestrial radiation.
keyPoints: Balance between incoming insolation and outgoing terrestrial radiation
Of 100 units: ~35 reflected (albedo), ~14 absorbed by atmosphere, ~51 absorbed by the surface
Surface re-radiates as long-wave terrestrial radiation
65 units absorbed = 65 units returned to space, so Earth's average temperature stays constant

text: State the factors that affect the distribution of temperature on the Earth's surface, and explain any three.
modelAnswer: Factors include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, slope and aspect of land, cloud cover and the nature of the surface. (1) Latitude: near the equator, the Sun's rays fall vertically and heat a small area intensely, so temperatures are high; towards the poles the rays become slanting, spread over a larger area and pass through more atmosphere, so temperatures decrease. (2) Altitude: temperature decreases by about 6.5 degrees C for every 1,000 m rise in height (normal lapse rate), because the atmosphere is heated from below by terrestrial radiation and the thinner air at higher altitudes holds less heat; hence hill stations are cooler. (3) Distance from the sea: the sea heats and cools more slowly than land, so coastal places have an equable (moderate) climate, while places far from the sea have an extreme (continental) climate with a large range of temperature. (4) Ocean currents: warm currents raise the temperature of coastal areas, while cold currents lower it.
keyPoints: Latitude: vertical rays at equator heat more; slanting rays at higher latitudes heat less
Altitude: temperature falls ~6.5 degrees C per 1000 m (normal lapse rate)
Distance from sea: coasts have equable climate; interiors have extreme climate
Ocean currents and winds: warm currents raise, cold currents lower coastal temperatures

text: How is an equable (maritime) climate different from a continental (extreme) climate?
modelAnswer: An equable climate is found in places near the sea. Because water heats up and cools down slowly, the sea keeps summers moderately cool and winters moderately warm, so the annual and daily range of temperature is small; the air is also more humid (e.g. Mumbai). A continental climate is found in places far from the sea, in the interior of continents. Since land heats and cools quickly and there is no moderating influence of the sea, summers are very hot and winters very cold, so the range of temperature is large, and the air is generally drier (e.g. Delhi).
keyPoints: Equable: near the sea, small range of temperature, mild summers and winters (e.g. Mumbai)
Continental: far from the sea, large range, very hot summers and very cold winters (e.g. Delhi)
Due to differential heating and cooling of land and water

text: State two effects of global warming. Give one way to control global warming.
modelAnswer: Global warming is the gradual rise in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere, caused mainly by the increase in greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and industry. Effects: (1) melting of glaciers and polar ice caps, leading to a rise in sea level and the flooding of low-lying coastal areas and islands; (2) changes in climate and rainfall patterns, causing more frequent droughts, floods, heat waves and cyclones, which affect agriculture and food supply; it also causes loss of biodiversity and the spread of diseases. Control measures: reduce the burning of fossil fuels by using renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), plant more trees (afforestation) and stop deforestation, use public transport, and save energy.
keyPoints: Cause: increase in greenhouse gases (CO2, methane) from fossil fuels and deforestation
Effect: melting ice caps and glaciers -> sea-level rise, coastal flooding
Effect: changing climate -> droughts, floods, heat waves; effects on agriculture and biodiversity
Control: renewable energy, afforestation, reduce fossil-fuel use

text: 'Inversion of temperature is a reversal of the normal lapse rate.' Justify the statement with an example.
modelAnswer: Normally, temperature decreases with increasing altitude at about 6.5 degrees C per km (the normal lapse rate). In an inversion of temperature, the opposite happens: temperature increases with height near the ground, so a layer of warm air lies over a layer of cold air. It usually occurs on long, clear, calm winter nights, when the ground loses heat rapidly by radiation and cools the air in contact with it. In mountainous regions, cold, dense air slides down the slopes and collects in the valley bottoms, so the valleys become colder than the slopes above. For example, in the hilly regions of Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh in winter, fruit orchards and settlements are located on the slopes rather than on the valley floors, which experience frost and fog.
keyPoints: Normal lapse rate: temperature falls ~6.5 degrees C/km with height
Inversion: temperature rises with height; warm air above cold air
Occurs on long, clear, calm winter nights; cold air drains into valleys
Example: valley floors in Kashmir/Himachal colder and foggy; orchards and settlements on slopes

text: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the pressure belts and the planetary wind system of the Earth.
modelAnswer: There are seven pressure belts. (1) Equatorial Low (Doldrums), 0-5 degrees N and S: intense heating causes air to rise, forming a low-pressure belt of calm, convergence of winds. (2) Sub-Tropical Highs (Horse Latitudes), around 30-35 degrees N and S: descending air from the upper atmosphere creates high pressure; winds diverge. (3) Sub-Polar Lows, around 60-65 degrees N and S: formed dynamically by the rotation of the Earth and the meeting of warm and cold winds. (4) Polar Highs, at 90 degrees N and S: very low temperatures make air dense and heavy, forming high pressure. Planetary winds blow from high to low pressure and are deflected by the Coriolis force: the Trade Winds (north-east in NH, south-east in SH) blow from the sub-tropical highs to the equatorial low; the Westerlies (south-west in NH, north-west in SH) blow from the sub-tropical highs to the sub-polar lows; and the Polar Easterlies blow from the polar highs to the sub-polar lows. A diagram would show the globe with these belts marked by latitude and arrows for each wind system.
keyPoints: Equatorial Low/Doldrums (0-5 degrees): rising air, calm
Sub-Tropical Highs/Horse Latitudes (30-35 degrees): descending air, divergence
Sub-Polar Lows (60-65 degrees) and Polar Highs (90 degrees)
Trade Winds: sub-tropical high -> equatorial low (NE in NH, SE in SH)
Westerlies: sub-tropical high -> sub-polar low; Polar Easterlies: polar high -> sub-polar low

text: State the differences between Tropical cyclones and Temperate cyclones.
modelAnswer: Tropical cyclones develop over warm tropical oceans (between about 5 and 25 degrees latitude) where the sea temperature is above about 27 degrees C, whereas temperate cyclones develop in the mid-latitudes (35-65 degrees) where warm and cold air masses meet along a front. Tropical cyclones are smaller in size but much more intense, with very high wind speeds (often above 120 km/h), a calm central 'eye', and very heavy rainfall; temperate cyclones cover a much larger area but have gentler winds and lighter, more widespread rainfall, and they have no eye. Tropical cyclones form mainly in late summer and autumn, move from east to west with the Trade Winds, and weaken quickly over land; temperate cyclones occur mostly in winter, move from west to east with the Westerlies, and can travel over both land and sea. Tropical cyclones are very destructive.
keyPoints: Tropical: over warm tropical oceans; Temperate: mid-latitudes, along fronts
Tropical: smaller, intense, very strong winds, calm eye; Temperate: larger, gentler, no eye
Tropical: move east to west with Trade Winds; Temperate: west to east with Westerlies
Tropical: weaken over land, very destructive; Temperate: travel over land and sea, widespread light rain

text: Heavy rains with gusty winds lashed parts of southern West Bengal as severe cyclonic storm 'Dana' made landfall on the Odisha coast in October 2024. (a) How is a cyclone different from an anticyclone? (b) What are tropical cyclones called in China and in Australia?
modelAnswer: (a) A cyclone is a low-pressure system with the lowest pressure at the centre; winds blow inwards towards the centre, anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, and it brings cloudy, stormy weather and heavy rain. An anticyclone is a high-pressure system with the highest pressure at the centre; winds blow outwards from the centre, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, and it brings calm, clear, dry weather. (b) In China (and Japan) tropical cyclones are called Typhoons; in Australia they are called Willy-willies (now also commonly called cyclones).
keyPoints: Cyclone: low pressure at centre, winds converge inwards, stormy weather
Anticyclone: high pressure at centre, winds diverge outwards, fine weather
NH: cyclone anticlockwise, anticyclone clockwise (reversed in SH)
China: Typhoons; Australia: Willy-willies

text: Explain the correlation between temperature and air pressure.
modelAnswer: Temperature and air pressure are inversely related. When air is heated, it expands, becomes lighter (less dense) and rises, so the pressure it exerts on the surface decreases, creating a low-pressure area; this is why the hot equatorial region has a permanent low-pressure belt. When air is cooled, it contracts, becomes denser and heavier and sinks, so the pressure increases, creating a high-pressure area; this is why the very cold polar regions have high-pressure belts. Thus, high temperature generally means low pressure and low temperature generally means high pressure.
keyPoints: Inverse relationship between temperature and pressure
Heated air expands, becomes lighter, rises -> low pressure (e.g. Equatorial Low)
Cooled air contracts, becomes denser, sinks -> high pressure (e.g. Polar Highs)

text: What is a Jet Stream? State two uses of it.
modelAnswer: A jet stream is a narrow belt of very fast-moving winds blowing from west to east in the upper troposphere, near the tropopause, at a height of about 9-14 km, with speeds that can exceed 300 km/h. Uses: (1) aircraft flying in the direction of the jet stream (west to east) save time and fuel, while flights in the opposite direction avoid it; (2) jet streams influence weather and climate, for example they help steer the movement of cyclones and anticyclones and influence the onset and withdrawal of the Indian monsoon, so studying them helps in weather forecasting.
keyPoints: Narrow belt of very fast west-to-east winds near the tropopause (9-14 km)
Aircraft flying with it save time and fuel
Influences weather: steers cyclones, affects Indian monsoon; useful for forecasting

text: Write two differences between the Doldrums and the Horse Latitudes.
modelAnswer: The Doldrums is the Equatorial Low-Pressure belt between about 0 and 5 degrees N and S, formed thermally by intense heating that causes air to rise; it is a zone of convergence where the Trade Winds meet, with calm conditions, high humidity and frequent convectional rainfall. The Horse Latitudes are the Sub-Tropical High-Pressure belts at about 30-35 degrees N and S, formed dynamically by the descent of air from the upper atmosphere; they are zones of divergence from which the Trade Winds and Westerlies blow out, with calm, dry and clear weather, which is why many of the world's hot deserts lie in these latitudes.
keyPoints: Doldrums: 0-5 degrees, low pressure, thermal origin, rising air, convergence
Horse Latitudes: 30-35 degrees, high pressure, dynamic origin, descending air, divergence
Doldrums: humid with convectional rain; Horse Latitudes: dry, clear, deserts

text: Smita and her family went to Little Andaman Island for a holiday. Every day the morning was clear, but by late afternoon the sky became dark with clouds and there was heavy rain. (a) What type of rainfall is this? (b) With the help of a diagram, explain how this type of rainfall occurs.
modelAnswer: (a) Convectional rainfall. (b) In equatorial and tropical regions like the Andaman Islands, the Sun shines almost vertically and the ground is heated intensely during the day. The air in contact with the hot surface warms, expands, becomes light and rises in convection currents, carrying a large amount of moisture evaporated from the surrounding seas. As it rises, it cools adiabatically; when it reaches its dew point, the water vapour condenses to form towering cumulonimbus clouds. By afternoon these clouds release heavy rain, often with thunder and lightning, which is why it is called the '4 o'clock shower'. After the rain the sky clears again. A diagram would show the heated ground, rising air currents, cooling and condensation into cumulonimbus clouds, and rain falling.
keyPoints: Type: convectional rainfall
Intense heating of the surface warms the air, which rises in convection currents
Rising moist air cools to dew point and forms cumulonimbus clouds
Heavy afternoon rain with thunder and lightning ('4 o'clock shower')

text: With the help of a diagram, explain the formation of orographic (relief) rainfall, and name a mountain range in India responsible for this type of rainfall.
modelAnswer: Orographic rainfall occurs when moist winds blowing from the sea meet a mountain barrier and are forced to rise along the windward slope. As the air rises, it expands and cools; on reaching the dew point, the water vapour condenses into clouds, and heavy rain falls on the windward side. After crossing the summit, the air descends the leeward slope; it gets compressed and warms up, its capacity to hold moisture increases, and it has already lost most of its moisture, so the leeward side receives very little rain. This dry area is called the rain-shadow area. In India, the Western Ghats cause heavy orographic rainfall on the western (windward) coast, e.g. Mumbai and Mangaluru, while the Deccan Plateau on the leeward side, e.g. Pune, lies in the rain shadow. A diagram would show moist winds rising up the windward slope, clouds and rain there, and dry descending air on the leeward slope.
keyPoints: Moist winds forced to rise over a mountain barrier on the windward side
Rising air cools to dew point, condenses -> heavy rain on windward side
Descending air on leeward side warms and is dry -> rain-shadow area
Example: Western Ghats (windward Mumbai wet, leeward Pune dry)

text: What do you mean by frontal (cyclonic) rainfall? State one characteristic of it.
modelAnswer: Frontal or cyclonic rainfall occurs when two air masses of different temperature and density meet along a boundary called a front. The warm, light, moist air is forced to rise over the cold, dense air; as it rises it cools, condenses and forms clouds, which give rainfall. It is associated with temperate cyclones and is common in the mid-latitudes (e.g. north-western Europe, and north-western India in winter through western disturbances). Characteristics: it is usually a steady, light to moderate drizzle spread over a large area and can continue for several days; it occurs mostly in winter, and the sky remains cloudy.
keyPoints: Warm air mass meets cold air mass along a front
Warm moist air is forced to rise over cold air, cools and condenses
Associated with temperate cyclones in mid-latitudes
Steady, widespread drizzle lasting several days, mostly in winter

text: Suggest a region in India where the relative humidity will be high, and give a reason for your answer.
modelAnswer: Relative humidity will be high in coastal regions such as Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, or in the north-eastern states like Assam and Meghalaya. Coastal areas are close to the sea, from which large amounts of water evaporate, so the air contains a lot of water vapour relative to its capacity; in the north-east, heavy rainfall, dense forests and nearness to the Bay of Bengal keep the air moist. Hence the air is close to saturation and relative humidity is high.
keyPoints: Coastal regions (e.g. Mumbai, Chennai) or north-east India (Assam, Meghalaya)
Nearness to the sea -> high evaporation, abundant water vapour
Heavy rainfall and forests keep the air moist; air close to saturation

text: Mention any two conditions necessary for condensation to take place.
modelAnswer: (1) The air must be cooled to its dew point, i.e. it must become saturated, which happens when moist air rises and cools, or comes into contact with a cold surface. (2) There must be hygroscopic nuclei, such as dust, smoke or salt particles, in the air, around which water vapour can condense into droplets. A high relative humidity (large amount of water vapour in the air) also favours condensation.
keyPoints: Air must be cooled to the dew point (saturation)
Presence of condensation nuclei: dust, smoke, salt particles
High relative humidity favours condensation

text: With reference to water pollution: (i) name any two sources, (ii) state two effects, and (iii) mention a preventive measure.
modelAnswer: (i) Sources: untreated industrial effluents containing chemicals and heavy metals; domestic sewage; agricultural runoff carrying pesticides and fertilizers; oil spills from ships; and dumping of garbage and plastics into water bodies. (ii) Effects: contaminated water spreads water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, jaundice and dysentery; excess nutrients cause eutrophication (algal bloom) that reduces oxygen and kills fish; toxic substances like mercury and cadmium accumulate in food chains and cause diseases (e.g. Minamata disease). (iii) Prevention: industrial effluents and sewage must be treated in treatment plants before release; reduce use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides; do not dump garbage or immerse idols in rivers.
keyPoints: Sources: industrial effluents, sewage, agricultural runoff, oil spills
Effects: water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid), eutrophication kills aquatic life
Toxic metals accumulate in the food chain
Prevention: treat sewage/effluents; limit fertilizers and pesticides; no dumping

text: Give two ways by which soil pollution affects human beings, and mention two ways in which toxic elements are absorbed into the soil.
modelAnswer: Toxic elements enter the soil through (1) excessive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture, and (2) dumping of industrial waste, mining waste and municipal solid waste (including plastics and e-waste); acid rain and irrigation with polluted water also add toxins. Effects on humans: (1) toxic chemicals are absorbed by crops and enter the food chain, causing diseases such as cancer, kidney and liver damage, and poisoning by heavy metals like lead and cadmium; (2) polluted soil lowers soil fertility and crop yields, affecting food supply, and contaminates groundwater used for drinking.
keyPoints: Toxins enter soil via excess fertilizers/pesticides
Toxins enter soil via industrial, mining and municipal waste (plastics, e-waste)
Effect: toxins enter food chain -> cancer, organ damage, heavy-metal poisoning
Effect: reduced fertility and yields; groundwater contamination

text: Give two effects of noise pollution, and mention a preventive measure.
modelAnswer: Effects: (1) prolonged exposure to loud noise can cause temporary or permanent hearing loss; (2) it causes stress, irritation, headaches, sleeplessness and high blood pressure, and reduces concentration and work efficiency. Noise also disturbs birds and animals. Prevention: use silencers on vehicles and machines, avoid the unnecessary use of horns and loudspeakers, plant trees along roads as noise barriers, and locate industries and airports away from residential areas.
keyPoints: Hearing loss from prolonged loud noise
Stress, headaches, sleeplessness, high blood pressure, lower concentration
Prevention: silencers, limit horns/loudspeakers, tree belts, zoning

text: Differentiate between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, with examples.
modelAnswer: Biodegradable waste is waste that can be broken down (decomposed) by natural agents such as bacteria and fungi into harmless substances within a short time; examples are kitchen waste, vegetable peels, paper, cow dung and dead leaves. It can be converted into useful products such as compost (manure) and biogas. Non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down by natural agents, or takes hundreds of years to do so, and therefore accumulates in the environment and causes long-term harm; examples are plastics, glass, metals, DDT and other pesticides, and radioactive waste. It must be reduced, reused or recycled.
keyPoints: Biodegradable: decomposed by microorganisms quickly (kitchen waste, paper)
Can be converted into compost and biogas
Non-biodegradable: not decomposed, persists for a long time (plastic, glass, metals)
Must be reduced, reused or recycled

text: Write a preventive measure for each of the following types of pollution: (i) Noise, (ii) Water, (iii) Soil.
modelAnswer: (i) Noise pollution: fit silencers to vehicles and machines, avoid the unnecessary use of horns and loudspeakers, and plant trees along roads to absorb sound. (ii) Water pollution: treat industrial effluents and sewage before releasing them into rivers, and avoid dumping garbage or washing clothes and cattle in water bodies. (iii) Soil pollution: reduce the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides by using organic manure and bio-fertilizers, and dispose of solid waste properly through segregation, recycling and sanitary landfills.
keyPoints: Noise: silencers, limit horns and loudspeakers, tree belts
Water: treat effluents and sewage before discharge; no dumping
Soil: organic manure/bio-fertilizers; proper waste segregation and recycling

text: Give reasons: (i) People living in urban areas are more prone to respiratory diseases. (ii) Nuclear waste needs to be disposed of very carefully. (iii) Lead is a source of pollution.
modelAnswer: (i) Urban areas have a large number of vehicles and industries that release smoke, dust, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides; this polluted air causes respiratory diseases such as asthma, bronchitis and lung infections. (ii) Nuclear waste is radioactive and remains harmful for thousands of years; if not disposed of safely (e.g. in sealed containers buried deep underground), radiation can leak into soil, water and air, causing cancer, genetic mutations and birth defects. (iii) Lead is released from batteries, paints, older leaded petrol and industries; it does not break down and accumulates in the body, damaging the brain, nervous system and kidneys, especially in children.
keyPoints: Urban air polluted by vehicles and industries -> asthma, bronchitis
Nuclear waste is radioactive for thousands of years; leaks cause cancer and mutations
Lead from batteries, paints, industry; accumulates in body, damages brain and kidneys

text: Differentiate between thermal metamorphism and dynamic metamorphism.
modelAnswer: Thermal (contact) metamorphism is caused mainly by the great heat of magma or lava coming into contact with surrounding rocks; it affects a small area around the intrusion (e.g. limestone changing into marble). Dynamic (regional) metamorphism is caused mainly by great pressure, along with heat, produced during earth movements such as folding and mountain building; it affects very large areas (e.g. shale changing into slate).
keyPoints: Thermal metamorphism: caused by heat of magma in contact with rocks
Thermal: limited area, e.g. limestone to marble
Dynamic metamorphism: caused by great pressure during earth movements
Dynamic: large regions, e.g. shale to slate

text: Write one point of difference each between: (a) Cyclones and Anticyclones, (b) Trade winds and Westerlies.
modelAnswer: (a) A cyclone is a low-pressure system in which winds blow inward towards the centre, anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, bringing cloudy and stormy weather. An anticyclone is a high-pressure system in which winds blow outward from the centre, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, bringing calm, clear weather. (b) Trade winds blow from the sub-tropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low (from the north-east in the Northern Hemisphere and south-east in the Southern Hemisphere), whereas the Westerlies blow from the sub-tropical highs towards the sub-polar lows (from the south-west in the Northern Hemisphere and north-west in the Southern Hemisphere).
keyPoints: Cyclone: low pressure at centre, winds blow inward, stormy weather
Anticyclone: high pressure at centre, winds blow outward, calm clear weather
Trade winds: sub-tropical high to equatorial low (NE and SE trades)
Westerlies: sub-tropical high to sub-polar low (SW and NW)

text: Write one point of difference each between: (a) Dew and Fog, (b) Fog and Mist.
modelAnswer: (a) Dew is formed when water vapour condenses as droplets on cool surfaces such as grass and leaves near the ground, whereas fog is formed when water vapour condenses on dust particles in the air close to the ground, forming a cloud at ground level that reduces visibility. (b) Fog is denser and reduces visibility to less than 1 km, whereas mist is thinner, contains fewer droplets and visibility is more than 1 km.
keyPoints: Dew: droplets condense on cool surfaces like grass
Fog: condensation on dust particles in the air near the ground, reducing visibility
Fog: visibility less than 1 km; dense
Mist: thinner; visibility more than 1 km

text: Differentiate between warm and cold ocean currents (two points).
modelAnswer: Warm currents flow from the low latitudes (equatorial regions) towards the higher latitudes, and their water is warmer than the surrounding water; they raise the temperature of the coasts they touch and bring rainfall (e.g. the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio). Cold currents flow from the higher (polar) latitudes towards the lower latitudes, and their water is colder than the surrounding water; they lower the temperature of the coasts and make them dry, sometimes causing fog (e.g. the Labrador, Oyashio, Peru currents).
keyPoints: Warm currents flow from equator towards poles; cold currents from poles towards equator
Warm currents raise coastal temperature and bring rain
Cold currents lower coastal temperature, cause dryness and fog
Examples: Gulf Stream (warm), Labrador Current (cold)

text: State two uses of lines of latitude.
modelAnswer: (1) Latitudes, together with longitudes, form the grid that helps to locate the exact position of any place on the Earth. (2) They help to divide the Earth into heat zones (torrid, temperate and frigid) and so indicate the general climate of a place. (3) They help to calculate distances in the north-south direction, as one degree of latitude is about 111 km.
keyPoints: Help locate places on the Earth along with longitudes (grid)
Divide the Earth into heat zones, indicating climate
Help measure north-south distances (1 degree is about 111 km)

text: Mention any two economic significances of rocks.
modelAnswer: (1) Rocks are the source of many valuable minerals and metals such as iron, copper, gold and bauxite. (2) Rocks such as granite, marble, sandstone and limestone are used as building materials, and limestone is used to make cement. (3) Sedimentary rocks contain fossil fuels such as coal, petroleum and natural gas. (4) Weathering of rocks forms soil, which is the basis of agriculture.
keyPoints: Source of minerals and metals
Building materials (granite, marble); limestone for cement
Sedimentary rocks contain coal, petroleum and natural gas
Weathered rocks form soil for agriculture

text: Give an overview of any two natural factors that cause earthquakes.
modelAnswer: (1) Movement of tectonic plates: when plates collide, move apart or slide past each other, stress builds up in the rocks; its sudden release along faults produces earthquakes, as in the Himalayan region. (2) Volcanic activity: the pressure of rising magma and the explosion of gases during an eruption shake the crust and cause earthquakes. (3) Faulting and folding: sudden movement of rock blocks along a fault releases energy as seismic waves.
keyPoints: Movement of tectonic plates builds and suddenly releases stress
Volcanic eruptions and rising magma shake the crust
Sudden slipping of rocks along faults

text: The shape and size of sand dunes depend upon several factors. Mention any three.
modelAnswer: The shape and size of sand dunes depend on: (1) the speed and direction of the wind (constant or variable); (2) the amount (supply) of sand available; (3) the presence of obstacles such as bushes, rocks or vegetation that make the wind drop its load; and (4) the nature of the ground surface over which the wind blows.
keyPoints: Velocity and direction of the wind
Quantity of sand available
Presence of obstacles such as rocks or vegetation
Nature of the ground surface

text: Explain any two factors affecting the work of a river.
modelAnswer: (1) Volume of water: a river with more water has greater energy and can erode and carry more load; the work increases during floods. (2) Velocity and gradient: a steep slope gives the river high velocity, so it erodes and transports more (as in the upper course), while on a gentle slope its speed falls and it deposits its load. (3) Load: the amount and type of material carried affects its ability to erode; a river carrying hard pebbles erodes its bed faster, but an overloaded river deposits material.
keyPoints: Volume of water: more water gives more energy
Velocity/gradient: steep slope means more erosion; gentle slope leads to deposition
Load carried affects erosion and deposition

text: Mention any two factors responsible for the formation of tides.
modelAnswer: (1) The gravitational pull of the Moon, and to a lesser extent the Sun, on the ocean waters; the Moon's pull is stronger because it is much closer to the Earth. (2) The centrifugal force produced by the rotation of the Earth-Moon system, which causes water to bulge on the side of the Earth opposite the Moon. (3) The rotation of the Earth, which brings each place under the tidal bulges in turn.
keyPoints: Gravitational pull of the Moon (and the Sun)
Centrifugal force causing a bulge on the opposite side
Rotation of the Earth brings places under the bulges

text: Discuss any two causes responsible for global warming.
modelAnswer: (1) Burning of fossil fuels such as coal, petroleum and natural gas in industries, power plants and vehicles releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat. (2) Deforestation reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide, so more of it remains in the atmosphere. (3) Other greenhouse gases such as methane (from paddy fields, cattle and landfills) and CFCs add to the trapping of heat.
keyPoints: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide
Deforestation reduces absorption of carbon dioxide
Methane and CFCs from farming, landfills and industry

text: State two characteristics of the revolution of the Earth.
modelAnswer: (1) The Earth moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit from west to east (anticlockwise as seen from above the North Pole). (2) It takes about 365 and a quarter days (one year) to complete one revolution, which is why a leap year is added every four years. (3) During revolution the Earth's axis remains tilted at 66.5 degrees to the plane of its orbit, which, with revolution, causes the change of seasons.
keyPoints: Earth moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit, west to east
One revolution takes about 365 1/4 days
Axis remains tilted at 66.5 degrees, causing seasons

text: State two properties of the lines of latitude.
modelAnswer: (1) Lines of latitude are parallel to the Equator and to each other and never meet. (2) They are complete circles that become smaller from the Equator towards the poles; the Equator is the longest and the only great circle among them. (3) They are drawn from west to east, and the distance between any two successive parallels is about 111 km.
keyPoints: Parallel to the Equator and to each other
Circles that become smaller towards the poles; Equator is the largest
Run east-west; about 111 km apart per degree

text: Differentiate between weathering and erosion.
modelAnswer: Weathering is the breaking down or decomposition of rocks in their original place (in situ) by temperature changes, frost, chemical reactions or living organisms; no movement of the material is involved. Erosion is the wearing away of the land surface and the removal and transportation of the broken material by moving agents such as running water, wind, glaciers and sea waves.
keyPoints: Weathering: breakdown of rocks in situ, no transport
Erosion: wearing away and removal of material
Erosion requires moving agents like water, wind, ice

text: Differentiate between quantitative and qualitative pollutants.
modelAnswer: Quantitative pollutants are substances that are naturally present in the environment but become pollutants when their quantity increases beyond a certain limit, e.g. carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Qualitative pollutants are substances that do not occur naturally in the environment and are added only by human activities, e.g. pesticides such as DDT, herbicides and fungicides.
keyPoints: Quantitative: occur naturally, harmful when their amount exceeds a limit
Example of quantitative: carbon dioxide
Qualitative: not found in nature, added by humans
Example of qualitative: DDT, pesticides

text: Differentiate between an intermont plateau and a volcanic plateau.
modelAnswer: An intermont (intermontane) plateau is a plateau enclosed partly or fully by mountain ranges, formed during the process of mountain building, e.g. the Tibetan Plateau. A volcanic (lava) plateau is formed by the spreading of layers of lava from fissure eruptions, which cool and solidify to form a flat, raised surface, e.g. the Deccan Plateau in India.
keyPoints: Intermont plateau: surrounded by mountains, formed with mountain building
Example: Tibetan Plateau
Volcanic plateau: formed by layers of lava from fissure eruptions
Example: Deccan Plateau

text: State three ways in which oceans are important to us.
modelAnswer: (1) Oceans are a major source of food such as fish and other sea food, and of minerals, salt and petroleum. (2) They provide cheap sea routes for international trade and transport. (3) They influence climate by moderating temperatures of coastal areas and are the main source of moisture for rainfall. (4) Tides and waves can be used to generate electricity, and coasts support tourism.
keyPoints: Source of food (fish), salt, minerals and petroleum
Cheap sea routes for trade and transport
Moderate climate and supply moisture for rainfall
Tidal energy and tourism

text: Discuss how individuals may reduce energy consumption to create a cleaner and eco-friendly world.
modelAnswer: Individuals can: (1) switch off lights, fans and appliances when not in use and use energy-efficient LED bulbs and star-rated appliances; (2) use public transport, car-pooling, bicycles or walking instead of private vehicles, which reduces fuel use and air pollution; (3) use renewable sources such as solar water heaters and solar panels; and (4) reduce, reuse and recycle materials, since manufacturing new goods consumes a great deal of energy.
keyPoints: Switch off unused appliances; use LED bulbs and efficient appliances
Use public transport, car pools, cycling or walking
Use solar and other renewable energy
Reduce, reuse and recycle
